Some say the first word was “bloom.” Others insist it was the sound a pinecone made when it struck the earth. In Danbury, where the bean fields lean against their orange fences, these are considered the same story.

Before that word, nothing knew quite how to begin. Seeds lay underground with their coats buttoned tight. The rivers waited in their beds. Even the wind, though it already had a postal address, had never received a letter.

Then a pinecone fell.

It struck a stone, and the stone answered, and between them came a small, rough syllable.

“Bloom.”

The pinecone split. A root entered the crack in the stone. Across the meadows, beans pushed up through the soil, followed by wheat and barley and several plants nobody had ordered. The rivers got out of bed. The wind hurried home to see whether anything had arrived.

There was one envelope beneath its door.

On the front, in a hand as fine as frost, someone had written: *To the Wind, wherever it is presently staying.*

Inside was the first word, folded once.

Now there is some disagreement about who sent it. The elders name Malfred, whom the Tonkerins call their savior. The gardeners credit the pinecone. The blades of Swordbreaker insist that a word capable of cracking stone must have been a scream, and Welldun has spent three hundred years accusing Deathmaker, who denies it with considerable irritation.

But the Drake family of Danbury keeps a different account. Their oldest grandmother said that Malfred found the word caught on an orange fence, trembling like a scrap of cloth. Rather than pocket it, he lifted it gently and sent it over.

“What was on the other side?” the children always asked.

“Nothing yet,” she told them. “That was why he sent it.”
